domains.name: Algebra
domains.spec: About 35% of the test: 13 to 15 of the 44 questions
domains.blurb: Straight lines in every costume: equations, functions, word problems, systems and inequalities.

domains.name: Advanced Math
domains.spec: About 35% of the test: 13 to 15 of the 44 questions
domains.blurb: Curves: parabolas, exponential growth, square roots, and rewriting expressions.

domains.name: Problem-Solving and Data Analysis
domains.spec: About 15% of the test: 5 to 7 of the 44 questions
domains.blurb: Rates, percentages, tables, graphs and chance: arithmetic with a story attached.

domains.name: Geometry and Trigonometry
domains.spec: About 15% of the test: 5 to 7 of the 44 questions
domains.blurb: Area and volume, angles, right triangles, and circles.

le1.name: Linear equations in one variable
le1.idea: One unknown, one equation. Peel the layers off the letter in reverse order until it stands alone.
le1.plain: An equation is a balance scale. Whatever you do to one side, do to the other, and the scale stays level. Undo the last thing that was done to x first: if x was multiplied by 3 and then had 5 added, subtract the 5 before you divide by 3.
steps: Clear brackets: multiply out anything in parentheses.
Move every x-term to one side and every plain number to the other.
Divide by the number in front of x.
Read the last line of the question again. If it asks for 2x or x + 4, do that last step.

example.q: If 5(x − 3) + 2 = 3x + 7, what is the value of x?

le1.trap: The extra step. “If 3x + 7 = 19, what is x + 4?” x is 4, and 4 is a choice; the answer is 8.
le1.tip: “No solution” and “infinitely many solutions” are not solving questions: line up the two sides and compare them (see the question type below).

lf.name: Linear functions
lf.idea: A linear function adds the same amount every time x goes up by 1. Two numbers describe it: the slope m and the starting value b.
lf.plain: f(x) is a machine: put a number in, one number comes out. f(4) means “feed it a 4”. In y = mx + b, m is the amount added per step (it follows words like per, each, every) and b is the amount you start with (a flat fee, a starting balance).
steps: Find the starting amount: that is b.
Find the per-step amount: that is m.
Write y = mx + b and say what x counts.
Put in the number you were given, or set y equal to the target and solve.

example.q: A gym charges a $40 joining fee plus $25 a month. What is the cost of 6 months?
lines: Starting amount b = 40, per month m = 25
example.check: Six months of fees is $150, plus the $40 fee: $190.

lf.trap: Slope and starting value swapped. Both numbers are in the question and both are in the choices. Check the units: the slope is “dollars per month”, the start is just “dollars”.
lf.tip: From a table, any two rows give the slope: change in y ÷ change in x. Walk the table back to x = 0 to read b.

le2.name: Linear equations in two variables
le2.idea: The same straight line, written in whatever form is least convenient. Convert it, read the slope, and know what parallel and perpendicular do.
le2.plain: Slope is steepness: how far up for each step across. Parallel lines climb at the same rate, so they have the same slope. Perpendicular lines meet at a right angle; their slopes are negative reciprocals (flip the fraction and change the sign), so the two slopes multiply to −1.
steps: If the line is in the form Ax + By = C, its slope is −A/B.
Parallel: copy the slope. Perpendicular: flip and change the sign.
x-intercept: put y = 0. y-intercept: put x = 0.
To test a point, put its x and y into the equation.

example.q: Line ℓ is 3x + 4y = 12. Line k is perpendicular to ℓ. What is the slope of k?

le2.trap: The negative reciprocal done halfway: flipping without changing the sign, or the reverse. Both halfway answers are offered.
le2.tip: In a word problem like 5x + 8y = 200, the numbers in front of x and y are prices or rates, and 200 is the total.

sys.name: Systems of two linear equations
sys.idea: Two lines. They cross once, never meet (parallel), or are the same line. You can tell which without solving.
sys.plain: A solution to a system is a point on both lines at once. Lines can do only three things: cross once (one solution), run side by side (no solution) or sit on top of each other (infinitely many).
steps: To find the crossing point: add or subtract the equations so one letter disappears, then solve for the other.
Put that value back in to get the second letter.
Read the question again: it often wants x + y, 2x, or only y.
On a hard one, graph both lines in Desmos and click the crossing point.

example.q: 3x + 2y = 19 and x − 2y = 1. What is x + y?
example.check: Check: 3(5) + 2(2) = 19 and 5 − 2(2) = 1. Both 5 and 2 are offered as choices; the answer is 7.

sys.trap: Answering with x when the question asks for x + y. You did the work right and stopped one step early.
sys.tip: If the question wants x + y, try adding the two equations first; the total often falls out in one line.

inq.name: Linear inequalities
inq.idea: An equation names one value; an inequality names a whole range. Often you can test a number instead of solving.
inq.plain: Everything works like an equation, with one exception: multiplying or dividing both sides by a negative number flips the sign, because it mirrors the number line.
steps: Translate the words: at least ≥, at most ≤, more than >, fewer than <, no more than ≤.
For “which inequality represents…”, test a number that clearly should work and one that clearly should not.
For “greatest number” questions, solve, then round in the direction the story allows (you cannot buy 12.6 tickets).
On a graph, a solid line means ≤ or ≥; a dashed line means < or >.

example.q: Small boxes weigh 20 lb, large boxes 50 lb, and a van carries at most 1,000 lb. Which inequality fits?
example.check: The inequality behaves the way the van does.

inq.trap: “At most” read as “at least”, and a sign not flipped after dividing by a negative. Both mirror-image answers are offered.
inq.tip: In a “greatest number of …” question, the exact answer is often a decimal. Round down if you cannot exceed the limit.

eqx.name: Equivalent expressions
eqx.idea: Two expressions are equivalent when they give the same answer for every x. You rewrite; you never solve.
eqx.plain: An expression has no equals sign, so there is nothing to solve. The question asks for a different-looking recipe that always gives the same result.
steps: Multiply out brackets and combine like terms; or factor (common factor first, then difference of squares, then the trinomial).
Exponents: xᵃ·xᵇ = xᵃ⁺ᵇ, (xᵃ)ᵇ = xᵃᵇ, x⁻ᵃ = 1/xᵃ, x^(a/b) = the b-th root of xᵃ.

Numerical substitution can eliminate mismatching choices. A unique matching option can identify the answer when one is guaranteed correct; matching alone is not an identity proof. Check the original domain.
Constants to find? Expand both sides and match the x² parts, the x parts and the plain numbers.

example.q: Which is equivalent to x² + 7x + 12? A (x+2)(x+6)  B (x+3)(x+4)  C (x+1)(x+12)  D (x−3)(x−4)
example.check: Factoring gives the same answer: two numbers that multiply to 12 and add to 7 are 3 and 4.

eqx.trap: The outside power not applied to the number in front: (2x³)⁴ is 16x¹², not 2x¹².
eqx.tip: Distinct expressions can agree at selected inputs. Avoid excluded values; algebra explains an identity for its full domain.

nle.name: Nonlinear equations and systems
nle.idea: Same unwrapping as a linear equation, but the letter is squared, under a root or in a fraction. Squaring can create false answers, so check yours.
nle.plain: Squaring loses a sign: 3 and −3 both square to 9, so x² = 9 has two answers. Squaring both sides of an equation can add an answer that never worked. That is why you put your answers back into the original equation.
steps: Get everything on one side so it equals 0.
Factor, or use the quadratic formula x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / 2a.
If you squared both sides or cleared a fraction, check each answer in the original equation.
Apply any condition in the question: positive, negative, the greater one.

example.q: What is the solution to √(x + 6) = x?
example.check: Only x = 3 works. The rejected −2 is a listed choice.

nle.trap: The extra root. When the question says “the positive solution”, both roots are in the choices.
nle.tip: “In terms of” questions want a formula, not a number. Check your rearrangement by putting in easy numbers.

nlf.name: Nonlinear functions
nlf.idea: The biggest skill on the test. Almost everything here is a parabola (from squaring) or an exponential curve (from repeated multiplying).
nlf.plain: A parabola is a symmetric U. Its turning point, the vertex, is where the maximum or minimum sits, exactly halfway between the two places it crosses the x-axis. Exponential growth multiplies by the same number each step: grows 8% means ×1.08, shrinks 15% means ×0.85.
steps: Know the three forms of a parabola: y = a(x − h)² + k shows the vertex (h, k); y = a(x − p)(x − q) shows the zeros p and q; y = ax² + bx + c shows the y-intercept c.
No vertex form? The vertex is at x = −b/(2a); put that x back in for the y-value.
Exponential: y = a·bˣ. a is the starting amount; b is the multiplier per step.
When a change happens every n years, the exponent is x/n.

example.q: f(x) = x² − 6x + 5. What is the minimum value of f?
example.check: The minimum value is −4, and it happens at x = 3. Both 3 and −4 are choices; the question asked for the value.

nlf.trap: The x of the vertex when the question asked for the maximum or minimum value, and the reverse. Say the sentence: “the minimum is −4, at x = 3”.
nlf.tip: Desmos marks a parabola’s vertex and zeros as grey points; click them. That turns most hard vertex questions into a quick read.

rat.name: Ratios, rates, proportions and units
rat.idea: A rate is a fraction with units on top and bottom. Write the units in and cancel them like numbers, and the setup checks itself.
rat.plain: “Per” means “divided by”. 60 miles per hour is 60 miles ÷ 1 hour. When you convert, multiply by fractions arranged so the unit you want to lose appears once on top and once on the bottom.
steps: Write what you have as a fraction with its units.
Multiply by conversion fractions so unwanted units cancel.
Stop when only the units the question asks for are left.
Proportions: put the same kind of thing on top on both sides, then cross-multiply.

example.q: A space station travels 4.76 miles per second. How many miles per hour is that?
example.check: If you divide by 3,600 instead, the units come out as nonsense. The unit check catches it.

rat.trap: Square and cubic units: 1 foot is 12 inches, but 1 square foot is 144 square inches and 1 cubic foot is 1,728 cubic inches.
rat.tip: Density = mass ÷ volume. Population density = people ÷ area. Same idea, different units.

pct.name: Percentages
pct.idea: Percent means “out of 100”. Every percentage question turns on one thing: the percent of what?
pct.plain: 30% is 30/100 is 0.30. “Is” means equals, “of” means times, “what” is the unknown. Going up 20% means multiplying by 1.20; going down 20% means multiplying by 0.80.
steps: Translate in reading order: “24 is what percent of 80” → 24 = (p/100) × 80.
Percent change = (new − old) ÷ old. Always divide by the old value.
Several changes in a row: multiply the multipliers. Never add the percents.
Working back to an original: divide by the multiplier (after 15% off, price ÷ 0.85).

example.q: A $200 jacket goes up 20%, then down 20%. What is the final price?
lines: Or at once: 1.20 × 0.80 = 0.96, a 4% net drop
example.check: The two 20% changes do not cancel: the drop is taken from a bigger number.

pct.trap: Dividing by the new value instead of the old one, and adding percents (20% up then 20% down is not zero).
pct.tip: a% of b equals b% of a. 4% of 75 is 75% of 4, which is 3.

1vd.name: One-variable data: center and spread
1vd.idea: The mean uses every numerical value. The median uses central ordered positions; removing or adding values can change those positions.
1vd.plain: Adding a constant shifts mean and median equally without changing spread. Multiplying all values by k scales standard deviation by |k|. Calculator stdev uses the sample convention; stdevp uses the population convention. Use the convention asked for.
steps: Median: put the values in order, then count to the middle position, (n + 1) ÷ 2.
Mean: total ÷ count. When a value is added or removed, work with totals: mean × count = total.
Range: largest − smallest.
From a frequency table, the values are the categories; the frequencies are how many times each appears.

example.q: Households (15 in all) own 0, 1, 2, 3 or 4 pets, with frequencies 2, 5, 4, 3, 1. What is the median?
lines: 0 pets fill positions 1–2, 1 pet fills 3–7, 2 pets fill 8–11
example.check: The median is 2 pets. Do not answer with a frequency.

1vd.trap: Answering with a frequency (how many households) instead of a value (how many pets).
1vd.tip: Five numbers average 12; what sixth number makes the average 14? Totals: 6 × 14 − 5 × 12 = 84 − 60 = 24.

2vd.name: Two-variable data: models and scatterplots
2vd.idea: The line of best fit answers almost every question here. The dots are there to make wrong answers.
2vd.plain: A scatterplot shows one dot per case. The line of best fit is the trend. “Predicted” or “estimated” means read the line, not a dot. A straight-looking cloud is a linear model; one that bends upward faster and faster is exponential.
steps: Predicted value: find x on the bottom axis, go up to the line, read across.
Slope: the change in y for each 1 added to x, with units.
Linear or exponential: equal differences mean linear; equal ratios mean exponential.
Average rate of change between two points: change in y ÷ change in x.

example.q: A line of best fit is y = 2.5x + 10. What does it predict when x = 8?
example.check: A dot near x = 8 might sit at 28 or 32; the prediction comes from the line.

2vd.trap: Reading a dot instead of the line; misreading the scale on the axes.
2vd.tip: Read the axis labels and the size of one grid square before you read any value.

prb.name: Probability and conditional probability
prb.idea: A probability is a fraction. The whole skill is choosing the right number for the bottom.
prb.plain: Probability = the outcomes you want ÷ all the outcomes in the group. Words like “given that”, “of those who” and “among the seniors” shrink the group: the bottom becomes that row or column total, not the grand total.
steps: Underline the group the question names: everyone, or only one row or column?
The bottom of the fraction is that group’s total.
The top is the cell that is in that group and has the feature asked about.
Check the answer form: fraction, decimal, or percent.

example.q: Of 160 students, 75 prefer cats; 45 of those are seniors. A cat-lover is picked at random. What is the probability the student is a senior?
example.check: 45 ÷ 160 would answer a different question (a random student who is a senior and prefers cats).

prb.trap: Using the grand total when the question restricted you to one row or column.
prb.tip: Expected count = probability × total. A 0.35 chance among 60 marbles means 21 marbles.

inf.name: Inference from samples and margin of error
inf.idea: A sample estimate plus or minus the margin of error gives a range of believable values for the whole population.
inf.plain: If 62% of a random sample agree, with a margin of error of 4%, the true figure is plausibly anywhere from 58% to 66%. Bigger samples give smaller margins of error.
steps: Range = estimate − margin to estimate + margin.
A conclusion must use the range, not one exact number.
Scale up from a random sample: sample share × population size.
Larger random sample → smaller margin of error.

example.q: A random sample of 400 city adults: 62% support a plan, margin of error 4%. Which conclusion is best?
lines: It applies to adults in this city only
example.check: “Exactly 62%” and “adults in the whole country” are both wrong.

inf.trap: Treating the estimate as exact, or applying it to a bigger group than the one sampled.
inf.tip: Larger random samples generally reduce margin of error under comparable confidence, variability and design; they do not automatically remove bias.

stc.name: Evaluating statistical claims
stc.idea: Two kinds of random. Random selection lets you generalize to the population sampled. Random assignment lets you claim cause and effect.
stc.plain: Pick people at random from a group, and the results describe that group and nobody else. Randomly decide who gets a treatment, and you can say the treatment caused the difference. Without random assignment you can only report a link.
steps: Who was sampled, and was it random? That is the largest group you can generalize to.
Were subjects randomly assigned to treatments? Only then can you claim cause.
A survey of volunteers or of one special place does not represent everyone.
Watch for samples that are biased by where or how they were taken.

example.q: A random sample of students at one school tried a game, and their scores improved. To whom do the results apply?
lines: Random selection from students at that school
So: students at that school, not all students everywhere
example.check: Choices that name a bigger population are wrong however good the numbers are.

stc.trap: Generalizing past the group that was sampled. It is offered in almost every one of these questions.
stc.tip: This skill has only 12 questions in the bank, but 7 are Hard; the rule above settles most of them.

av.name: Area and volume
av.idea: The formulas are printed on the reference sheet. Most questions give you the area or volume and ask for a length.
av.plain: Area counts unit squares; volume counts unit cubes. A prism or cylinder is its base area times its height. A cone or pyramid is one third of that.
steps: Find the shape’s formula on the reference sheet.
Put in everything you know, including the area or volume if it is given.
Solve for the missing length.
Scale: multiply every length by k and areas multiply by k², volumes by k³.

example.q: A cone has volume 48π cubic feet and height 9 feet. What is its radius?

av.trap: Using the diameter where the radius belongs, and dropping the 1/3 from a cone or pyramid.
av.tip: Shaded region = whole shape − the part cut out.

lat.name: Lines, angles and triangles
lat.idea: A short list of angle rules does almost all the work. Learn the list and this is the most mechanical skill on the test.
lat.plain: Where two lines cross, opposite angles are equal and side-by-side angles add to 180°. When a line crosses two parallel lines, the same set of angles repeats at both crossings. A triangle’s angles add to 180°. Similar triangles have the same angles, so their sides are in proportion.
steps: Mark every angle you know on the figure.
Use: vertical angles equal; straight line 180°; triangle 180°; around a point 360°.
Parallel lines: corresponding and alternate angles are equal; same-side interior angles add to 180°.
Similar triangles: find the scale factor from one pair of matching sides, then apply it.

example.q: Two similar triangles: sides 6 and 8 in the first, 9 and x in the second. What is x?

lat.trap: Matching the wrong sides in similar triangles. Match sides by the angles they face.
lat.tip: An exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the two inside angles not next to it.

rtt.name: Right triangles and trigonometry
rtt.idea: Mostly Hard, but most of it collapses if you spot a familiar triangle before calculating.
rtt.plain: Pythagoras: a² + b² = c², where c is the side across from the right angle. sin = opposite ÷ hypotenuse, cos = adjacent ÷ hypotenuse, tan = opposite ÷ adjacent. The two small angles add to 90°, so the sine of one equals the cosine of the other.
steps: Look for a known triangle: 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17, 7-24-25 and their multiples.
Special triangles (on the reference sheet): 45-45-90 is 1 : 1 : √2; 30-60-90 is 1 : √3 : 2.
Label opposite and adjacent from the angle you are using.
sin(x°) = cos(90° − x°).

example.q: Right triangle ABC, right angle at C, AC = 9 and BC = 12. Find AB and sin A.
lines: 9 and 12 are 3 and 4 times 3, so AB = 15

rtt.trap: Opposite and adjacent read from the wrong angle; sine and cosine swapped.
rtt.tip: If a question gives sin of one small angle and asks for cos of the other, the answer is the number you were given.

cir.name: Circles
cir.idea: About 6 in 10 circle questions are about the circle’s equation in the xy-plane. The rest are arcs, radians and tangent lines.
cir.plain: (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r² is Pythagoras for every point on the circle: center (h, k), radius r. If the equation comes multiplied out, complete the square. An arc is a fraction of the whole circle: (angle ÷ 360) × circumference. 180° is π radians.
steps: Read the center from the brackets, changing each sign: (x − 3)² means x = 3; (y + 4)² means y = −4.
The right side is r², not r: 36 means radius 6.
Expanded equation: halve the x-number and square it; do the same for y; add both to each side.
Arcs and sectors: (central angle ÷ 360°) × the whole circumference or area.

example.q: x² + y² − 6x + 8y − 11 = 0. What are the center and radius?
example.check: Check a point: (3, 2) is 6 above the center. (0)² + (6)² = 36.

cir.trap: Reporting r² as the radius (36 instead of 6), and reversing the signs of the center.
cir.tip: A radius drawn to the point where a tangent line touches meets that line at 90°.

le1-count.name: How many solutions? (one variable)
le1-count.spot: “How many solutions…”, “no solution”, “infinitely many solutions”, often with a constant to find.
steps: Simplify both sides to the form ax + b.
Same x-number and same plain number: infinitely many solutions.
Same x-number, different plain number: no solution.
Different x-numbers: exactly one solution.
le1-count.trap: Trying to solve for x. With matching x-parts, x cancels and there is nothing to find.
le1-count.tip: To find a constant: set the x-numbers equal (and the plain numbers equal for “infinitely many”, unequal for “no solution”).

le1-model.name: Build the equation from a story
steps: Name the unknown in words.
Write each sentence of the story as a piece of the equation.
Test a choice with small easy numbers from the story if two look alike.
le1-model.trap: A choice that uses the right numbers in the wrong places (rate and fixed amount swapped).

le1-word.name: One-step story problem
le1-word.spot: A short story with one unknown: books shared out, a perimeter, a total cost.
steps: Write one equation from the story.
Solve it.
Check the answer makes sense in the story (a whole number of people, a positive length).
le1-word.trap: Answering with an in-between number, such as the total before the last step.

le1-solve.name: Solve the equation
le1-solve.spot: “What value of x is the solution…?” or “If …, what is the value of …?”
steps: Multiply out brackets; clear fractions by multiplying both sides by the bottom number.
Get x-terms on one side, numbers on the other.
Divide. Then check the question asks for x and not something built from x.
le1-solve.trap: The value of x offered when the question asked for an expression such as 3x − 2.

lf-interpret.name: What does this number mean?
lf-interpret.spot: “What is the best interpretation of 25 in this context?”
steps: Is the number multiplied by x? Then it is the change per one unit of x (slope).
Is it on its own? Then it is the value when x = 0 (starting value).
Pick the choice with matching units.
lf-interpret.trap: A choice that describes the starting value when the number is the rate, or the reverse.

lf-intercept.name: Find an intercept
lf-intercept.spot: “What is the x-intercept / y-intercept of the graph of f?”
steps: y-intercept: set x = 0.
x-intercept: set y (or f(x)) = 0 and solve.
From a graph or table, read where the line crosses the axis.
lf-intercept.trap: x- and y-intercepts swapped. Both points are offered.

lf-model.name: Linear model from a story
lf-model.spot: Fees, rates, “per”, “each”: “Which function gives the total cost…?”
steps: The one-time amount is b.
The amount per unit is m.
Write y = mx + b; check a value against the story.
lf-model.trap: Fixed amount and rate swapped; a rate that should only start after the first hour or day.

lf-table.name: Linear function from a table
lf-table.spot: A table of x and f(x) values.
steps: Slope = change in f(x) ÷ change in x between any two rows.
Walk back to x = 0, or put one row into y = mx + b, to find b.
Check the formula on a third row.
lf-table.trap: Using one row’s ratio y/x as the slope.

lf-graph.name: Linear function from a graph
lf-graph.spot: “The graph of the linear function f is shown.”
steps: Find two points where the line crosses grid corners exactly.
Slope = rise ÷ run between them.
Read b where the line crosses the y-axis.
lf-graph.trap: Misreading the scale: check what one grid square is worth on each axis.

lf-build.name: Line through given points
lf-build.spot: “The graph contains the points (…) and (…). Which equation defines f?”
steps: Slope = (y₂ − y₁) ÷ (x₂ − x₁).
Put one point into y = mx + b to find b.
Test the other point in your answer.
lf-build.trap: Subtracting the coordinates in different orders on top and bottom.

lf-eval.name: Evaluate the function
lf-eval.spot: “The function f is defined by … What is f(3)?” or “For what value of x does f(x) = 10?”
steps: f(3): put 3 wherever x appears and work it out.
f(x) = 10: set the formula equal to 10 and solve for x.
lf-eval.trap: Mixing up the input and the output: f(3) is an output; “f(x) = 3” gives an input.

le2-parallel.name: Parallel and perpendicular lines
le2-parallel.spot: “Line k is parallel / perpendicular to line ℓ…”
steps: Get the slope of the given line (from y = mx + b, or −A/B from Ax + By = C).
Parallel: same slope. Perpendicular: flip and change the sign.
If a point is given, use it to find b.
le2-parallel.trap: Flipping without changing the sign, or changing the sign without flipping.

le2-interpret.name: Meaning of a number in a two-variable equation
le2-interpret.spot: “What is the best interpretation of 8 in this context?”
steps: See what the number multiplies: it is the amount per one of those.
A number on the other side of the equals sign is usually the total.
Match the units in the choices.
le2-interpret.trap: A choice that swaps the meaning of the two letters.

le2-model.name: Two-variable equation from a story
le2-model.spot: “Which equation represents this situation?” with two kinds of items and a total.
steps: Each kind: price (or size) × how many.
Add them and set equal to the total.
Check which letter stands for which item.
le2-model.trap: The prices attached to the wrong letters.

le2-intercept.name: Slope and intercepts of a line
le2-intercept.spot: “What is the slope…?”, “What is the y-intercept…?” of a given equation.
steps: Rewrite as y = mx + b, or use slope = −A/B from Ax + By = C.
y-intercept: put x = 0. x-intercept: put y = 0.
le2-intercept.trap: Reading the coefficient of x as the slope before y is on its own.

le2-point.name: Points, tables and graphs of a line
le2-point.spot: “Which table…”, “What is an equation of the graph shown?”, “The point (a, 5) lies on the line…”
steps: A point is on a line if its x and y make the equation true.
For a graph, read two exact points and find the slope and intercept.
For tables, test one row in each choice; one wrong row rules a choice out.
le2-point.trap: A table where only some rows fit.

le2-solve.name: Use the given equation
le2-solve.spot: A two-variable equation from a story, and the value of one letter.
steps: Put the known value in.
Solve for the other letter.
le2-solve.trap: Putting the value in for the wrong letter.

sys-count.name: How many solutions? (system)
sys-count.spot: “No solution”, “infinitely many solutions”, “exactly one solution”, often “where k is a constant”.
steps: For genuine lines A₁x+B₁y=C₁ and A₂x+B₂y=C₂, compute A₁B₂−A₂B₁.
A nonzero determinant gives exactly one solution.
If zero, check consistency by elimination: an impossible constant gives none; equivalent equations give infinitely many.
First handle equations with both variable coefficients zero; avoid dividing by zero in coefficient ratios.
sys-count.trap: Starting to solve. These questions are built so that solving wastes time.
sys-count.tip: Same slope, different intercept = no solution. Same slope, same intercept = infinitely many.

sys-model.name: Build the system from a story
sys-model.spot: “Which system of equations could be used to find…?”
steps: One equation counts things (how many in total).
The other counts money, weight or points.
Check that each number sits beside the right letter.
sys-model.trap: A system where the count equation uses the prices.

sys-graph.name: System on a graph
sys-graph.spot: “The graph of a system is shown. What is the solution?” or “At how many points do the graphs intersect?”
steps: The solution is the point where the lines cross.
Read it exactly from grid corners.
Parallel lines never cross: no solution.
sys-graph.trap: Reading an intercept instead of the crossing point.

sys-word.name: Two-unknown story problem
sys-word.spot: Tickets of two prices, two mixtures, a total count and a total cost.
steps: Write a count equation and a value equation.
Solve (elimination is usually quickest).
Answer the quantity asked about.
sys-word.trap: Answering with the other unknown, which you also found.

sys-solve.name: Solve the system
sys-solve.spot: “The solution to the given system is (x, y). What is the value of …?”
steps: Line up the equations. If one letter has matching or opposite numbers, add or subtract to remove it.
Otherwise get one letter alone and substitute it into the other equation.
Answer exactly what is asked: x, y, x + y, 2x − y.
sys-solve.trap: Giving x when the question asked for y or for x + y.
sys-solve.desmos: Type both equations and click the crossing point.

inq-graph.name: Shaded region
inq-graph.spot: “The shaded region represents the solutions to which inequality?”
steps: Solid boundary: ≤ or ≥. Dashed: < or >.
Test a point in the shaded region, such as (0, 0) if it is shaded.
inq-graph.trap: The right line with the wrong side shaded.

inq-point.name: Which point or table satisfies it?
inq-point.spot: “Which point is a solution…”, “For which table are all values solutions…?”
steps: Put each point into the inequality.
One failing row rules out a whole table.
inq-point.trap: Treating the boundary as allowed when the sign is < or >.

inq-maxmin.name: Greatest or least number allowed
inq-maxmin.spot: “What is the greatest number of … possible?” “What is the minimum number…?”
steps: Write the inequality from the story.
Solve it as if it were an equation.
Round in the direction the story allows: down for a maximum of whole items, up for a minimum.
inq-maxmin.trap: Rounding the wrong way (12.6 tickets allowed means 12, not 13).

inq-model.name: Write the inequality
steps: Translate: at least ≥, at most ≤, more than >, less than <.
Build the expression for the total.
Test an easy value that should be allowed.
inq-model.trap: Keep at least/at most and the units straight. The presence of a particular distractor is not guaranteed.

eqx-coef.name: Match the coefficients
eqx-coef.spot: “… is equivalent to ax² + bx + c, where a, b and c are constants. What is …?”
steps: Expand the given side completely.
Match the x² parts, the x parts and the plain numbers.
Solve the small equations that result.

eqx-exp.name: Exponents and roots
eqx-exp.spot: Powers, roots or fractional exponents: “for all positive values of x…”
steps: Write roots as fractional powers: the cube root of x⁴ is x^(4/3).
Multiply: add exponents. Divide: subtract. Power of a power: multiply.
Rewrite the answer in the form the choices use.
eqx-exp.trap: Adding exponents when you should multiply them, or the reverse.

eqx-rational.name: Fractions with x
eqx-rational.spot: Fractions with x in the bottom.
steps: Find a common bottom.
Combine the tops.
Simplify, and note values of x that are not allowed.

eqx-rewrite.name: Which expression is equivalent?
steps: Multiply out brackets and combine like terms, or factor.
Watch every minus sign: −(x − 3) is −x + 3.
Unsure? Put x = 2 into the original and each choice.
eqx-rewrite.trap: A sign lost when multiplying out a bracket that starts with a minus.
eqx-rewrite.tip: Test values can eliminate alternatives; coinciding at one value does not prove equivalence. Retain the domain when cancelling factors.

nle-literal.name: Rearrange a formula (“in terms of”)
nle-literal.spot: “Which equation correctly expresses h in terms of V and r?”
steps: Find what is attached to the target letter.
Undo it step by step, doing the same to both sides.
Check with easy numbers: pick values, compute, and see if your formula gives them back.
nle-literal.trap: Choosing a number. The answer is a formula.

nle-count.name: How many real solutions?
nle-count.spot: “How many distinct real solutions…”, “exactly one solution”, “no real solutions”.
steps: Identify the actual equation and its domain before transforming it.
For ax²+bx+c=0 with a≠0, the discriminant distinguishes two, one or zero distinct real roots.
A parameter making a=0 requires a separate linear/constant case.
After squaring or clearing denominators, filter transformed roots through the original equation. Higher-degree and absolute-value equations need their own root-count reasoning.
nle-count.trap: Solving fully when only the number of solutions is asked.

nle-sum.name: Sum or product of the solutions
nle-sum.spot: “What is the sum of the solutions…?”
steps: For a genuine quadratic ax²+bx+c=0 with a≠0, sum roots=−b/a and product=c/a, counting multiplicity.
Check whether the requested roots must be real, distinct or satisfy the original equation’s domain. Squaring and clearing denominators can introduce excluded roots.
nle-sum.trap: Forgetting to divide by a when a is not 1.
nle-sum.tip: Use the target coefficient relation only after confirming it describes the roots the question asks for.

nle-system.name: Line meets curve
nle-system.spot: A system with a squared term, or “the graphs intersect at…”
steps: Set the two expressions for y equal.
Solve the quadratic.
Put x back in to get y if asked.
nle-system.trap: Giving the x-coordinate when the y-coordinate was asked.
nle-system.desmos: Graph both and click the crossing points.

nle-sign.name: The positive (or negative) solution
nle-sign.spot: “What is the positive solution…?”, “the greater of the two…”
steps: Find the real solutions the original equation permits.
Apply the required sign, order and domain restriction.
nle-sign.trap: Do not assume there are exactly two roots or that a rejected root appears among the choices.

nle-radical.name: Square roots and fractions
nle-radical.spot: An equation with √ or with x in a denominator.
steps: Get the root alone, then square both sides (or multiply by the denominator).
Solve.
Check every answer in the original equation and throw out any that fail.
nle-radical.trap: Keeping an extraneous answer that only works in the squared equation.

nle-solve.name: Solve a quadratic or other nonlinear equation
nle-solve.spot: “What is a solution to the given equation?”
steps: Get 0 on one side.
Factor, or use the quadratic formula.
With choices: put each choice in; you need only one that works.
nle-solve.trap: Stopping at a factored form and reading the signs wrong: (x − 3) = 0 means x = 3.

nlf-transform.name: Shifts of a graph
steps: Up k: add k to the whole function. Down: subtract.
Right h: replace x with (x − h). Left: (x + h).
nlf-transform.trap: Right shifts use a minus sign inside the bracket.

nlf-vertex.name: Maximum, minimum and vertex
steps: Vertex form a(x − h)² + k: the vertex is (h, k).
Otherwise x = −b/(2a), or halfway between the zeros.
The maximum or minimum VALUE is the y-coordinate; it happens AT the x-coordinate.
nlf-vertex.trap: Giving the x of the vertex when the question wanted the value, or the reverse.
nlf-vertex.desmos: Graph it and click the grey vertex point.

nlf-exp-int.name: Meaning of an exponential model
nlf-exp-int.spot: “What is the best interpretation of 1.06 in this context?”
steps: The number in front is the starting value.
The base b: above 1 grows by (b − 1)×100% per step; below 1 shrinks by (1 − b)×100%.
Check what one step is (a year, a month).

nlf-exp.name: Build the exponential model
steps: Start amount = a.
Up p%: b = 1 + p/100. Down p%: b = 1 − p/100. Doubles: 2. Halves: 1/2.
Every n units: exponent x/n.
nlf-exp.trap: Using the rate (0.08) instead of the multiplier (1.08), or 0.15 instead of 0.85.

nlf-height.name: Height over time
nlf-height.spot: An object launched, thrown or dropped; height in feet or meters after t seconds.
steps: Height at a time: put in t.
Hits the ground: set height = 0 and keep the positive t.
Highest point: the vertex.
nlf-height.trap: The time of the highest point given when the height was asked.

nlf-interpret.name: Meaning of a number in a nonlinear model
nlf-interpret.spot: “Which of the following is the best interpretation of …?”
steps: Work out what the expression represents in the story (a length, a width, a count).
Match the units.
nlf-interpret.trap: A choice describing a different part of the same formula.

nlf-zeros.name: Zeros and x-intercepts
steps: Set f(x) = 0.
In factored form a(x − p)(x − q), the zeros are p and q.
If p is a zero, (x − p) is a factor.
nlf-zeros.trap: The sign flip: a factor (x + 4) means a zero at −4.

nlf-yint.name: y-intercept and points on the graph
nlf-yint.spot: “The graph has a y-intercept of …” or “passes through the point …”, often with constants.
steps: y-intercept: put x = 0.
A point on the graph: put its x and y into the equation to find the constant.
nlf-yint.trap: Putting the point’s coordinates into the wrong letters.

nlf-graph.name: Read a graph or table of a curve
nlf-graph.spot: “The graph of f is shown…”, “Which table gives values for…?”
steps: Read exact points from grid corners or table rows.
Check intercepts and whether the curve opens up or down.
Test choices with one or two points.
nlf-graph.trap: Misreading the scale of the axes.

nlf-geom.name: Area or volume as a function
nlf-geom.spot: A rectangle or box whose length is written in terms of its width.
steps: Write the area or volume formula with the expressions.
Multiply out, or set equal to the given value and solve.
Keep the positive length.

nlf-eval.name: Evaluate a nonlinear function
nlf-eval.spot: “The function f is defined by … What is f(…)?”
steps: Put the number in for x everywhere.
Order of operations: powers before multiplying.
For f(x + 2), replace every x with (x + 2).

rat-density.name: Density
steps: density = amount ÷ space (mass ÷ volume, people ÷ area).
Rearrange for what is missing.
Find the volume or area first if a shape is described.
rat-density.trap: Using a side length where the volume belongs.

rat-convert.name: Unit conversion
rat-convert.spot: “How many inches…”, “in feet per second”, “What is the depth in feet?”
steps: Write the conversion as a fraction equal to 1 (12 inches / 1 foot).
Arrange it so the old unit cancels.
Chain several if needed.
rat-convert.trap: Multiplying when you should divide. Units that do not cancel show the mistake.

rat-square.name: Square or cubic units
rat-square.spot: An area in square feet to square yards; a volume in cubic units.
steps: Square the length conversion for areas (1 yd² = 9 ft²).
Cube it for volumes (1 ft³ = 1,728 in³).
rat-square.trap: Using the plain length conversion (3 instead of 9).

rat-ratio.name: Ratios and proportions
rat-ratio.spot: “The ratio of a to b is 3 to 5…”, “proportional relationship”.
steps: Write the ratio as a fraction.
Set it equal to the second fraction with the same order.
Cross-multiply.
rat-ratio.trap: Flipping one ratio but not the other.

rat-rate.name: Speed and other rates
rat-rate.spot: “at a constant speed of…”, “per hour”, “at this rate”.
steps: distance = rate × time (and the same shape for any rate).
Make the time units match before you multiply.

rat-other.name: Rates written as expressions
rat-other.spot: A proportion written with letters: “Which expression gives the amount for…?”
steps: Find the amount for 1 unit first.
Multiply by the number of units asked for.

pct-change.name: Percent increase and decrease
steps: Change: multiply by (1 + p/100) or (1 − p/100).
Percent change = (new − old) ÷ old.
Several changes: multiply the multipliers.
Find the original: divide by the multiplier.
pct-change.trap: Dividing by the new value; adding percents across several changes.

pct-of.name: Percent of a number
pct-of.spot: “What is 30% of 80?”, “What percent of … is …?”, “How many of the items…”
steps: Translate: is → =, of → ×, percent → ÷ 100.
Solve the equation.
Check the answer is sensible (part smaller than whole if under 100%).
pct-of.trap: Finding the percentage when the question asked for the count, or the reverse.

1vd-change.name: What happens when a value is added or removed
1vd-change.spot: “If the highest score is removed…”, “A sixth value is added…”
steps: Work with totals: mean×count=total.
Recompute the central ordered positions for the median; an extreme deletion has no universal small effect.
Adding a value equal to the mean leaves the mean unchanged.
1vd-change.trap: Averaging two means without weighting them by count.

1vd-spread.name: Range and standard deviation
steps: Range = largest − smallest.
Standard deviation: compare only. More bunched around the middle = smaller.
1vd-spread.trap: Thinking adding the same number to every value changes the spread.

1vd-median.name: Median
steps: Put the values in order.
Middle position: (n + 1) ÷ 2. With an even count, average the middle two.
In a frequency table, count up through the frequencies.
1vd-median.trap: Answering with a frequency instead of a value.

1vd-mean.name: Mean (average)
steps: Mean = total ÷ count.
From a frequency table: multiply each value by its frequency, add, divide by the total frequency.
Missing value: total needed − total you have.
1vd-mean.trap: Dividing by the number of rows in a frequency table instead of the total frequency.

1vd-read.name: Read a chart, dot plot or box plot
1vd-read.spot: Bar charts, dot plots, box plots and frequency tables.
steps: Read axes and frequencies first.
A box spans Q1 to Q3, with the median inside. Follow the specified whisker/outlier convention rather than assuming every whisker is an extreme.
Answer the requested statistic, not the frequency of that value.
1vd-read.trap: Reading the wrong bar or the wrong axis.

2vd-predict.name: Predict from the line of best fit
2vd-predict.spot: “predicted by the line of best fit”, “closest to the estimated…”
steps: Find the x-value on the bottom axis.
Go up to the LINE, not to a dot.
Read across to the y-axis, or put x into the line’s equation.

2vd-slope.name: Meaning of the slope
2vd-slope.spot: “best interpretation of the slope of the line of best fit”.
steps: Slope = predicted change in y for each 1-unit increase in x.
Use the axis units in your sentence.
2vd-slope.trap: A choice that says “actual” instead of “predicted”, or swaps x and y.

2vd-model.name: Choose the best model
2vd-model.spot: “Which equation is the most appropriate model?”, “What type of function best models…?”
steps: Rising or falling? That fixes the sign of the slope.
Where does the trend cross the y-axis? That fixes b.
Straight trend: linear. Curving faster and faster: exponential.
2vd-model.trap: A choice with the right slope but the wrong starting value.

2vd-rate.name: Average rate of change
2vd-rate.spot: “average rate of change from … to …”, “greatest increase”.
steps: Change in y ÷ change in x between the two points.
Steeper segment = faster change.

2vd-read.name: Read the scatterplot or graph
2vd-read.spot: “How many…”, “Which of the following is true about…” a plotted data set.
steps: Read the axes and scale.
Find the exact data point or count the points asked about.

prb-closest.name: Closest to a fraction of a subgroup
prb-closest.spot: A category’s count should be closest to a stated fraction of a restricted total.
steps: Find the total of the named subgroup.
Multiply this total by the target fraction.
Compare each eligible category count with that target using absolute differences.
prb-closest.trap: Use the total female population, not the exhibit total, and compare female counts rather than each species’ female percentage.
prb-closest.desmos: Optional: 180/3 gives the target 60. Compare distances 1,33,6,20.
worked: One third of the 180 female penguins is 60. Female counts are 59 chinstrap,27 emperor,54 gentoo,40 macaroni. Their distances from 60 are 1,33,6,20, so chinstrap is closest.

prb-missing.name: Recover a missing cell or total
prb-missing.spot: A table contains a question mark or x, sometimes together with a known probability.
steps: If the whole is known, subtract all the other disjoint cells from it. Do not subtract margins as well as their cells.
If a probability is known, write wanted count / restricted total = given probability. Include x in that total if it belongs there.
Solve and check that the reconstructed counts satisfy the table and probability.
prb-missing.trap: Do not use the grand total when the given chance applies only to one row.
prb-missing.desmos: Optional equation check: 2/(10+8) equals 1/9. Solve the short equation by hand.
worked: Only rhesus-negative people may be selected. Their row total is 7+2+1+x=10+x, and 2 have type B. Therefore 2/(10+x)=1/9, so 18=10+x and x=8. The positive-rhesus row is irrelevant.

prb-symbolic.name: Write probability with a variable
prb-symbolic.spot: Counts include a letter and the answer is requested “in terms of” that letter.
steps: Use the variable count for the wanted category.
Add all categories to form the total, keeping the expression symbolic.
Write wanted / total; test a small positive value if choices look similar.
prb-symbolic.trap: Wanted / other is a ratio of categories, not a probability. The total must include the wanted category too.
prb-symbolic.desmos: No calculator needed. As a check, setting n=12 should give 1/2.
worked: There are n nonfiction books and 12 fiction books. The total is n+12, so P(nonfiction)=n/(n+12). The expression n/12 compares nonfiction to fiction instead of to all books.

prb-counting.name: Count integers satisfying every condition
prb-counting.spot: A randomly chosen integer must be even and within a stated range.
steps: Count all possible integers in the original set; endpoints matter.
Count only integers satisfying every requested property. Listing a short pattern can establish the count.
Divide qualifying count by original set size unless the question explicitly conditions on a subset.
prb-counting.trap: “Even and at most 50” does not change the denominator to 50 when selection is from 1 through 160.
prb-counting.desmos: Optional arithmetic: 25/160. No combinatorics command is needed for this bank’s question.
worked: 9ce8cbbe
The set has 160 numbers, 1 through 160. Favorable numbers are 2,4,…,50, which gives 25 outcomes. Therefore P(even and at most 50)=25/160=5/32, not 25/50.

prb-percent.name: A conditional percent
prb-percent.spot: “What percent of states with…” restricts the denominator and asks for percent units.
steps: Identify the group following “of”.
Divide the wanted subset by that group’s total.
Multiply by 100 and round the percent to the requested precision.
prb-percent.trap: 6/50=12% uses all states. A conditional percent here uses only the 45 sales-tax states.
prb-percent.desmos: Optional: 100*6/(39+6), then round the displayed percent to one decimal place.
worked: 5dc386fb
The states with a sales tax number 39+6=45. Of these, 6 have no income tax. The requested percent is (6/45)×100=13.333…%, or 13.3% to the nearest tenth.

prb-pooled.name: A condition spans several rows or categories
prb-pooled.spot: “At least”, “not in group 2”, or a condition across repeated rows requires combining several cells.
steps: Translate the condition into all eligible categories, including boundary values.
Add or build the eligible counts; multiply each per-row count by its number of rows before pooling.
Inside that eligible group, add the wanted counts and divide by the eligible total. Percentages may replace counts when they share one whole.
prb-pooled.trap: Do not average group probabilities: groups can contribute different numbers of eligible objects. “At least 10” includes both 10–19 and 20+.
prb-pooled.desmos: Optional: (5*9)/(6*8+5*9). Parentheses keep the full eligible sum in the denominator.
worked: e438ec3f

Among trees at least 20 feet tall, birches contribute 6×8=48 and maples contribute 5×9=45. There are 93 eligible trees, so P(maple | tall)=45/93=15/31. Using 9/(8+9) ignores the different numbers of rows.

prb-given.name: One restricted row or column
prb-given.spot: “Given that”, “of the”, or “if the person works in…” names the group you may choose from.
steps: Read the restriction first and mark that row or column.
Add within that restricted group to get the denominator.
Use only the wanted members inside that same group as the numerator.
prb-given.trap: Reversing the condition changes the denominator: P(master’s | HR) differs from P(HR | master’s).
prb-given.desmos: Optional: 2/(4+2) evaluates the HR example. The reading decision comes first.
worked: The condition is Human Resources. HR has 4 bachelor’s and 2 master’s employees, so its total is 6. The wanted count is 2: P(master’s | HR)=2/6=1/3. Using 2/8 would reverse the condition; 2/15 would describe a joint event.

prb-complement.name: Not, neither, or the remaining category
prb-complement.spot: The requested category is excluded from other named categories, or is the leftover group.
steps: Keep the sampling group fixed.
For “not A”, subtract A’s count or probability from the total or 1. For “neither blue nor yellow”, count every remaining color.
If a count is requested, multiply the remaining probability by the total.
prb-complement.trap: A remaining probability such as 0.28 is not the requested number of people. Subtract category probabilities only when those categories cannot overlap.
worked: 1fc4f47b
Each customer is in exactly one of theaters A, B, C. P(C)=1-0.48-0.24=0.28. With 350 customers, C contains 0.28×350=98 customers. The answer is 98, not 28.

prb-count.name: Turn a probability or rate into a count
prb-count.spot: The question gives a chance and total but asks “how many”, or gives a daily rate before asking for a fraction.
steps: Write wanted count = probability × matching total.
Use the total from the correct date and retain units such as millions.
If a rate must first produce a count, multiply rate × time, then divide by the named whole. Round only as requested.
prb-count.trap: A probability is a fraction, not a count. Extra historical totals may be irrelevant.
prb-count.desmos: Optional: 0.43*97 gives 41.71; round to 42 only because the question requests the nearest integer.
worked: September has 97 million subscribers and MTN’s probability is 0.43. Thus p=0.43×97=41.71 million, so p rounds to 42. The earlier 83-million total is not the September denominator.

prb-joint.name: Two features on one selection
prb-joint.spot: One object must satisfy both descriptions; the selection is still from the whole table.
steps: Find the intersection cell where both descriptions hold.
Add all disjoint cells if the grand total is not printed.
Divide the intersection count by the grand total.
prb-joint.trap: “Camping but no bicycle paths” is two features of one park, not a condition that limits selection to camping parks. Do not multiply probabilities without evidence of independence.
worked: Five parks have camping facilities and no bicycle paths. All parks total 20+5+8+4=37, so the probability is 5/37. The tempting 5/25 would apply only if the selected park were already known to have camping.

prb-simple.name: One feature: count over total
prb-simple.spot: A single draw asks for one color, category, sign, or row/column total.
steps: Name the entire group being sampled. “At random” describes the selection; it does not shrink this group.
Count every member with the requested feature, adding across rows or columns if needed.
Divide that count by the group total. Give a decimal or fraction when percent is excluded.
prb-simple.trap: A two-way table does not automatically make the question conditional. A row total can be the numerator over the grand total.
prb-simple.desmos: Optional arithmetic: type 13/(13+37). Desmos cannot choose the group for you.
worked: There are 13 red pens and 37 blue pens. The total is 50, so P(red)=13/(13+37)=13/50=0.26. The denominator is all pens, not just the 37 blue pens.

inf-moe.name: Margin of error
inf-moe.spot: “with an associated margin of error of…”, “plausible”, “most appropriate conclusion”.
steps: Range = estimate ± margin.
The conclusion must be about the population sampled, and use the range.
Bigger random sample → smaller margin.

inf-estimate.name: Scale a sample up to the population
inf-estimate.spot: “Based on the sample, what is the best estimate of the number of … in the city?”
steps: Sample share = count in sample ÷ sample size.
Estimate = share × population size.

stc-general.name: Who do the results apply to?
stc-general.spot: “What is the largest population to which the results can be generalized?”
steps: Find the group the sample was randomly chosen from.
That group, no bigger, is the answer.
stc-general.trap: A bigger group than the one sampled.

stc-design.name: Is the study or survey sound?
stc-design.spot: “Which of the following is true about the survey?”, “Which inference is appropriate?”
steps: Random selection? Then you may generalize to that population.
Random assignment? Then you may claim cause.
Volunteers or one special location: biased.

av-scale.name: Scaling a shape
av-scale.spot: “each side is 3 times…”, “the length and width are increased by…”, similar shapes.
steps: Lengths × k → areas × k², volumes × k³.
A percent increase in each length: multiply area by (1 + p/100)².
av-scale.trap: Area k² and volume k³ scaling require uniform similarity. If only one dimension changes, compute from the actual formula.

av-surface.name: Surface area
av-surface.spot: “surface area” of a box or prism.
steps: Sketch the faces: a box has 3 pairs of matching rectangles.
Add the area of every face. Leave out any face the question removes (no lid).
av-surface.trap: Giving the volume, or counting a missing lid.

av-volume.name: Volume of solids
av-volume.spot: Cylinders, cones, spheres, prisms, pyramids: volume given or asked.
steps: Formula from the reference sheet (cone and pyramid have 1/3).
Put in everything known.
Solve for the missing length if the volume is given.
av-volume.trap: Dropping the 1/3, or using the diameter.

av-perimeter.name: Perimeter
steps: Add all the sides.
Use the equal sides of squares and equilateral triangles.

av-area.name: Area of flat shapes
av-area.spot: Rectangles, triangles, squares, circles: “What is the area…?”, or the area is given.
steps: Formula from the reference sheet.
Put in what you know.
Solve for what is missing.
av-area.trap: Triangle area without the ½; diameter used as radius.

lat-similar.name: Similar and congruent triangles
steps: Match corresponding vertices from the order of the letters.
Scale factor = matching side ÷ matching side.
Angles stay the same; lengths multiply by the scale factor.
lat-similar.trap: Matching sides that are not in corresponding positions.

lat-parallel.name: Parallel lines and a transversal
lat-parallel.spot: “Line ℓ is parallel to line m…”
steps: Angles in the same position at each crossing are equal.
Z-shaped (alternate) angles are equal.
Same-side inside angles add to 180°.
lat-parallel.trap: Setting two angles equal when they actually add to 180°.

lat-lines.name: Intersecting lines
lat-lines.spot: “Two lines intersect at a point…”, vertical angles, a line extended.
steps: Opposite (vertical) angles are equal.
Angles on a straight line add to 180°.

lat-triangle.name: Angles in triangles and polygons
lat-triangle.spot: Triangle angle measures, isosceles or equilateral triangles, exterior angles, polygons.
steps: Triangle angles add to 180°.
Isosceles: the angles opposite the equal sides are equal.
Exterior angle = the two far inside angles added.
Polygon angle total = 180(n − 2).
lat-triangle.trap: Forgetting that the base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal.

rtt-complement.name: sin of one angle = cos of the other
rtt-complement.spot: Two acute angles that add to 90°; sin given, cos asked (or the reverse).
steps: sin(x°) = cos(90° − x°).
If sin A = cos B, then A + B = 90°.
rtt-complement.trap: sin A=cos B implies complementary angles under suitable restrictions, such as acute angles in a right triangle; it is not an unrestricted identity about angle sums.

rtt-trig.name: Sine, cosine and tangent
rtt-trig.spot: “sin”, “cos”, “tan” of an angle in a right triangle.
steps: Label opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse from the named angle.
SOH: sin = opp/hyp. CAH: cos = adj/hyp. TOA: tan = opp/adj.
Missing side? Use the triple or Pythagoras first.
rtt-trig.trap: Labelling the sides from the wrong angle.

rtt-special.name: 30-60-90 and 45-45-90 triangles
rtt-special.spot: Angles of 30°, 45° or 60°; isosceles right triangles; equilateral triangles; squares.
steps: 45-45-90: legs x, x; hypotenuse x√2.
30-60-90: short side x, long side x√3, hypotenuse 2x.
Cut an equilateral triangle in half to get two 30-60-90 triangles.

rtt-similar.name: Similar right triangles
rtt-similar.spot: A right triangle with a parallel line or a second triangle inside it.
steps: Equal angles mean similar triangles.
Set up matching sides in proportion, or use equal trig ratios.
rtt-similar.trap: Matching sides by position on the page instead of by angle.

rtt-pythag.name: Pythagorean theorem
rtt-pythag.spot: A right triangle with two sides known; “hypotenuse”, “diagonal”.
steps: Look for a known triple (3-4-5, 5-12-13) and its multiples.
Otherwise a² + b² = c², with c across from the right angle.
Leave the answer as a root if the choices do.
rtt-pythag.trap: Adding the squares when the missing side is a leg (subtract instead).

cir-radians.name: Radians and degrees
steps: 180° = π radians.
Degrees to radians: × π/180. Radians to degrees: × 180/π.
On the unit circle, a point at angle θ is (cos θ, sin θ).

cir-arc.name: Arcs, sectors and circumference
steps: Arc length = (angle ÷ 360) × 2πr.
Sector area = (angle ÷ 360) × πr².
In radians: arc length = r × angle.
cir-arc.trap: Using the area formula for an arc length.

cir-tangent.name: Tangent lines
cir-tangent.spot: “tangent to the circle at the point…”
steps: The radius to the point of tangency is perpendicular to the tangent.
Use a negative reciprocal only for a finite nonzero radius slope; a horizontal radius gives a vertical tangent and vice versa.
cir-tangent.trap: Using the radius’s slope as the tangent’s slope.

cir-transform.name: Shifted or resized circles
cir-transform.spot: “Circle B is circle A shifted down 3”, “same center, twice the radius”.
steps: Read circle A’s center and radius.
Shift the center; scale the radius.
Write the new equation, squaring the new radius.
cir-transform.trap: Doubling r² instead of r (twice the radius makes r² four times as big).

cir-build.name: Write the circle’s equation
cir-build.spot: “Which equation represents a circle with center … and radius …?”
steps: Write (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r².
Square the radius.
If a point on the circle is given, the radius is its distance from the center.
cir-build.trap: Writing r instead of r² on the right side.

cir-read.name: Center and radius from the equation
cir-read.spot: “What is the radius / center of the circle with equation …?”
steps: (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r²: center (h, k), radius √(right side).
Multiplied-out equation: complete the square for x and for y.
Diameter = 2 × radius.
cir-read.trap: r² given as the radius; center signs reversed.
cir-read.desmos: Normalize to x²+y²+Dx+Ey+F=0. The center is (−D/2,−E/2), and r²=(D²+E²)/4−F. These formulas also work for fractional centers. A graph is a check; r²<0 is no real circle, r²=0 is a point.

cir-geo.name: Circle figures
cir-geo.spot: A figure with a circle, radii and a triangle; “What is the value of x?”
steps: All radii are equal, so triangles from the center are isosceles.
Use triangle angle sums and any right angles at tangent points.
cir-geo.trap: Assuming the figure is drawn to scale when it says it is not.

le1-solve.entry: For 5(x-3)+2=3x+7, enter y=5(x-3)+2 and y=3x+7. Select the intersection; its x-coordinate is 10. Then evaluate any requested expression, e.g. 2(10)+1.
le1-solve.check: Both sides must agree at the reported x. Widen the x-window if the intersection is off screen; the default window cannot establish no solution.

le1-count.entry: Reduce to (a-c)x=d-b. If a-c is nonzero there is one solution; if it is zero, compare d-b with zero. For a parameter, first solve a-c=0 and then check the constant difference.
le1-count.check: A zero coefficient is a case to inspect before dividing: 0x=0 allows every real x; 0x=7 allows none.

le1-model.entry: Make a two-column ledger: fixed amount and amount per item. For a $12 fee plus $4 per item, test the proposed equation at 0 items ($12) and 1 item ($16).
le1-model.check: Tests can reject choices but do not generally prove an identity. The equation must also follow the story and use the stated domain.

le1-word.entry: For a $12 fee plus $4 each totaling $60, enter y=12+4x and y=60. Read x=12 at their intersection.
le1-word.check: Label x before entering anything; check nonnegative or integer restrictions and compute the final quantity requested.

lf-eval.entry: Enter f(x)=3x-7, then f(4) for an output. To find an input producing 11, graph y=f(x) and y=11 and select their intersection.
lf-eval.check: An intersection is an ordered pair: input first, output second. A constant function may have no matching input or every input.

lf-model.entry: If a tank has 80 liters at t=3 and loses 5 liters per minute, use V(t)=80-5(t-3). Evaluate V(3) and V(4) before expanding.
lf-model.check: The coefficient outside a shifted input is still a rate; the written constant 80 is the amount at t=3, not necessarily at t=0.

lf-interpret.entry: For C(t)=40+25(t-2), compute C(2)=40 and C(3)-C(2)=25. Attach units: dollars at month 2, and dollars per additional month.
lf-interpret.check: A standalone number need not be the initial value when the input is shifted. Read the complete expression and the time origin.

lf-intercept.entry: Enter f(x)=2x-6 and f(0). Graph y=f(x) and y=0 to locate the x-intercept (3,0).
lf-intercept.check: For f(x)=0 every x is a zero; for a nonzero constant there is none. Report a coordinate or a single value as requested.

lf-table.entry: Enter the given inputs and outputs in a table with columns x_1 and y_1. Enter y_1~m x_1+b. Read the fitted m and b; verify every listed row.
lf-table.check: Exact linear data should fit all rows, apart from numerical roundoff. An approximate regression does not prove exact linearity; repeated x values with different outputs cannot define a function.

lf-graph.choose: Hand: use widely separated exact points
lf-graph.entry: Record two labeled points from the line, with the actual axis units. For (2,7) and (8,19), compute (19-7)/(8-2)=2, then 7-2(2)=3.
lf-graph.check: More separation reduces reading error. Use exact marked coordinates when supplied; a screenshot does not turn an approximate grid reading into an exact value.

lf-build.entry: Through (2,7) and (8,19), write y-7=((19-7)/(8-2))(x-2). Expand only if the choices require it.
lf-build.check: If the two x-coordinates agree, the line is vertical; it cannot be written as a linear function y=f(x). Identical points alone do not determine a unique line.

le2-parallel.entry: For Ax+By=C, a parallel line has proportional normal vector (A,B). A perpendicular line can use normal vector (-B,A). Example: perpendicular to 3x+4y=12 through (1,2) is -4x+3y=2.
le2-parallel.check: This also handles horizontal and vertical lines. The slope formula -A/B requires B nonzero, and a proper line requires (A,B) not both zero.

le2-model.entry: For $3 small items and $5 large items totaling $30, use 3s+5l=30. Test the all-small endpoint (10,0) and all-large endpoint (0,6).
le2-model.check: Endpoints help detect swapped coefficients. Counts must also be nonnegative integers; the full line includes points the story excludes.

le2-interpret.entry: In 3s+5l=30, solve l=6-(3/5)s. The 5 is dollars per large item; -3/5 is the change in large-item count per extra small item at fixed total.
le2-interpret.check: A coefficient in standard form is not automatically a slope. Distinguish the units of the original coefficient from those of the rearranged rate.

le2-intercept.entry: For Ax+By=C, test (0,C/B) when B is nonzero and (C/A,0) when A is nonzero. Compute slope -A/B only when B is nonzero.
le2-intercept.check: x=0 is the whole y-axis, so its y-intercepts are not a unique point. A zero or inconsistent equation is not a proper line.

le2-point.entry: Put candidate points in table columns x_1,y_1. For 2x+3y=12, enter 2x_1+3y_1-12. Every residual must be 0 for the entire table to fit.
le2-point.check: A single zero residual certifies only that point. Inspect every row and preserve the coordinate order.

le2-solve.entry: For 4x+2y=18 with x=3, evaluate y=(18-4(3))/2. If the question instead asks 2y, calculate 18-4(3) directly.
le2-solve.check: Never divide by a coefficient before checking it is nonzero. A zero remaining coefficient gives either no solution or no unique value.

sys-solve.entry: Enter 3x+2y=19 and x-2y=1 directly. Select (5,2), then evaluate the requested expression, such as 2(5)-2.
sys-solve.check: Substitute both coordinates into both original equations. Expand the graph window around the expected scales if needed; rounded display coordinates need an exact check.

sys-count.entry: For a_1 x+b_1 y=c_1 and a_2 x+b_2 y=c_2, calculate D=a_1 b_2-a_2 b_1. D nonzero means one solution. If D=0, eliminate a variable and inspect the remaining constant equation.
sys-count.check: Avoid coefficient ratios, which can divide by zero. First handle 0x+0y=0 (no constraint) and 0x+0y=c with c nonzero (impossible).

sys-model.entry: Write one row per condition and one column per unknown. For 10 tickets at $3 or $5 costing $42, rows are s+l=10 and 3s+5l=42.
sys-model.check: Every term in a row must have the same units. Not every system story has a count equation: two mixtures may instead give two mass constraints.

sys-graph.choose: Hand: distinguish coincidence from no visible crossing
sys-graph.entry: Use two labeled points to recover each line when exact values are available. Compare slopes and intercepts algebraically rather than judging nearly parallel pixels.
sys-graph.check: Parallel distinct lines have no solution; coincident lines have infinitely many. A crossing outside the displayed graph still counts.

sys-word.entry: For 10 tickets, $3 basic and $5 premium, total $42: all-basic cost would be $30. The $12 excess buys $2 upgrades, so there are 6 premium tickets and 4 basic.
sys-word.check: This works when the count is fixed and both unit prices are constant. Check both the total count and total value.

inq-model.choose: Hand: test the boundary and nearby values
inq-model.entry: For at most $50 with a $10 fee and $4 each, write 10+4x<=50. Test x=10, then x=11, then x=0.
inq-model.check: Boundary equality must be allowed for at most/at least. A few numerical tests support rejection but the wording establishes the direction.

inq-maxmin.entry: For 10+4x<50, x<10, so the greatest whole number is 9. Test 9 and 10 in the original inequality. For x>10 the least whole number is 11.
inq-maxmin.check: Strict bounds require special care when the boundary is an integer. Include nonnegative and any other constraints before rounding.

inq-point.entry: For 2x+3y<=12 and candidate (3,2), evaluate 2(3)+3(2) and compare 12<=12. Repeat for every row of a proposed table.
inq-point.check: Equality works only for <= or >=. For a system of inequalities, each point must satisfy every inequality.

inq-graph.entry: Enter the candidate inequality exactly, for example y>2x-3. Compare boundary style and a known shaded point from the problem.
inq-graph.check: The origin is useful only if it is off the boundary and its shading is unambiguous. For vertical boundaries use x<c rather than a slope formula.

eqx-rewrite.choose: Hand plus Desmos: falsify then establish
eqx-rewrite.entry: Define f(x) as the original and g(x) as a choice. Compare f(2),g(2), then another allowed input to eliminate mismatches. Establish the survivor by expansion or factoring.
eqx-rewrite.check: Agreement at one input does not prove identity. Agreement at d+1 distinct inputs proves equality of polynomials of degree at most d only when that degree bound is established.

eqx-coef.choose: Hand: recover quadratic coefficients from values
eqx-coef.entry: If an expression is known to be quadratic f(x)=ax^2+bx+c, calculate c=f(0), b=(f(1)-f(-1))/2, and a=(f(1)+f(-1))/2-c.
eqx-coef.check: This uses the known degree bound; it is not valid for an unrestricted function. Preserve all parameter conditions and check the expanded expression.

eqx-exp.entry: For positive x, x^(1/2)x^(3/2)=x^2. For unrestricted real x, sqrt(x^2)=abs(x), not x. Use positive nonunit test values to reject wrong choices.
eqx-exp.check: Fractional exponent rules need compatible real domains. Negative bases may make roots undefined in real arithmetic; a calculator decimal is not an algebraic proof.

eqx-rational.entry: For (x^2-9)/(x-3), record x!=3 before factoring to x+3. For sums, multiply each numerator by the missing denominator factors before combining.
eqx-rational.check: Cancellation removes factors, never terms across addition. The simplified expression agrees with the original only on the original domain; its graph may hide a hole.

nle-solve.choose: Desmos: original left and right sides
nle-solve.entry: For x^2-3x=4, graph y=x^2-3x and y=4. Read x=-1 and x=4 at the intersections.
nle-solve.check: Graphing reports numerical candidates; verify in the original. An empty default window does not prove no roots; use algebra to establish the total count.

nle-sign.entry: For 2x^2-3x-2=0, factor (2x+1)(x-2)=0, giving -1/2 and 2. Identify positive, negative, greater, or lesser only after listing both.
nle-sign.check: Zero is neither positive nor negative. Radical and rational equations may reject one candidate on substitution, so filter before ordering.

nle-literal.entry: From V=pi r^2 h, h=V/(pi r^2) requires r!=0. From A=s^2 with s a length, s=sqrt(A), using A>=0 and s>=0.
nle-literal.check: Division by a parameter may discard a zero case. Squared unknowns can need both signs unless the story imposes nonnegativity; Desmos is not a symbolic equation solver.

nle-count.choose: Hand: discriminant with a degree check
nle-count.entry: Reduce to ax^2+bx+c=0. For a!=0, D=b^2-4ac gives 2,1,0 distinct real roots as D is positive, zero, negative. Solve the corresponding inequality when a parameter is involved.
nle-count.check: If a=0, inspect bx+c=0 separately. For rational or squared equations, excluded or extraneous roots can change the original equation’s count.

nle-sum.entry: For 3x^2-5x-2=0, sum of the two roots is 5/3 and product is -2/3. If real solutions are required, first check D>=0.
nle-sum.check: Requires a nonzero quadratic coefficient. These are the roots of that polynomial with multiplicity; excluded roots from a denominator or squaring must be removed before summing original solutions.

nle-system.entry: Enter y=x^2 and y=2x+3. The intersections are (-1,1) and (3,9). Substitute to get x^2-2x-3=0 if exact coordinates are needed.
nle-system.check: A system may have multiple intersections; use algebra to confirm completeness. Do not assume every nonlinear system reduces to a quadratic.

nle-radical.entry: For sqrt(x+6)=x, require x>=0 before squaring. Squaring gives (x-3)(x+2)=0; only 3 survives. For fractions, list all denominator zeros first.
nle-radical.check: Every candidate must satisfy the original equation. Graph the original sides if checking numerically; squaring alone loses sign information.

nlf-eval.entry: Enter f(x)=2(x-3)^2+1. Then enter f(-2), f(1+2), or f(f(0)) exactly as asked, using parentheses around negative inputs.
nlf-eval.check: f(x+2) changes the input and f(x)+2 changes the output. A function may be undefined at a requested input because of roots or denominators.

nlf-vertex.entry: For f(x)=-2x^2+8x+1, calculate h=-8/(2(-2))=2 and f(2)=9. On a restricted interval compare this value, if h is in the interval, with endpoint values.
nlf-vertex.check: A quadratic requires a!=0. A vertex outside the allowed domain is not the domain’s extremum; an open endpoint may give a bound that is never attained.

nlf-exp.entry: Doubling every 3 days from 50 gives P(t)=50*2^(t/3). To convert to a daily multiplier calculate 2^(1/3), then daily percent 100(2^(1/3)-1).
nlf-exp.check: Use positive bases for a continuous real exponential model. The initial amount occurs at t=0 only when the exponent is zero there; do not add successive percentages.

nlf-exp-int.entry: For P(t)=80*1.06^(t/2), calculate P(t+2)/P(t)=1.06. It represents 6% growth per 2 units of time; per-unit growth is 100(sqrt(1.06)-1) percent.
nlf-exp-int.check: The base’s time period comes from the whole exponent. A constant before a shifted exponent need not be the amount at time zero.

nlf-height.entry: For h(t)=-16t^2+64t+5, enter y=-16x^2+64x+5 {x>=0}. Locate the vertex and positive ground intersection; evaluate y at the vertex for the height.
nlf-height.check: Restrict to the modeled time interval, usually from launch until impact. Ground level may be a value other than zero, and the launch itself can be a zero-time root.

nlf-interpret.choose: Hand: use a dimensioned input check
nlf-interpret.entry: For A(w)=w(2w+3), annotate w as width and 2w+3 as length. At w=2, these give 2 and 7 length units, hence area 14 square units.
nlf-interpret.check: A product’s constant is not automatically a starting amount. Interpret the requested factor or coefficient within the entire model and its units.

nlf-zeros.entry: For f(x)=2(x-1)^2(x+3), zeros are 1 and -3; the even-multiplicity zero at 1 touches the axis without crossing.
nlf-zeros.check: The leading factor must be nonzero. A rational function’s canceled factor may be a hole rather than a zero; denominator zeros are excluded.

nlf-yint.entry: For f(x)=3*2^(x-1)+4, enter the function then f(0), giving 5.5. For an unknown scale a passing through (2,10), solve 10=a*2^(2-1)+4 by hand.
nlf-yint.check: A graph has a y-intercept only if x=0 is in its domain. The written additive constant need not be the intercept.

nlf-graph.entry: Enter a candidate f(x), then create a table and put in the exact x-values given by the problem. Compare all corresponding outputs, including signs and turning behavior.
nlf-graph.check: A few matching points do not prove two arbitrary curves identical. Check the stated function family, domain, and all distinguishing information.

nlf-transform.entry: Enter f(x)=x^2, then g(x)=f(x-3)+2. The original point (0,0) moves to (3,2). Compare a second point, such as (1,1) moving to (4,3).
nlf-transform.check: Changes inside the input act horizontally. For g(x)=f(kx), nonzero k scales horizontal coordinates by 1/k; account for reflection if k<0.

nlf-geom.choose: Hand plus Desmos: restrict feasible lengths
nlf-geom.entry: A 10-by-16 sheet with corner squares x cut out has V(x)=x(10-2x)(16-2x), with 0<x<5. Graph y=x(10-2x)(16-2x) {0<x<5}.
nlf-geom.check: Positive x alone is insufficient: every remaining dimension must be positive. A cubic volume model is not a quadratic; compare all feasible candidates.

rat-convert.entry: For 4.76 miles/second to miles/hour, enter 4.76*3600. Write (miles/second)*(3600 seconds/hour) alongside the entry.
rat-convert.check: Cancel the units before calculating; use the supplied conversion rather than a rounded remembered constant.

rat-square.entry: For 72 square feet to square yards, enter 72/(3^2)=8. For 2 cubic feet to cubic inches, enter 2*12^3=3456.
rat-square.check: Area uses a squared length factor and volume a cubed one; do not square the measured area itself.

rat-ratio.entry: For a:b=3:5 and total 64, write a=3k,b=5k, so 8k=64 and a=24. For a:b=3:5 with b=40, use 5k=40.
rat-ratio.check: Identify whether the known quantity is one part or the combined total. Ratios require a nonzero denominator.

rat-rate.entry: For 30 miles at 20 mph and 30 miles at 60 mph, enter (30+30)/(30/20+30/60)=30 for the overall mph.
rat-rate.check: Average speed is total distance divided by total time, including stops when relevant; averaging speeds directly works only for equal time intervals.

rat-density.entry: For a cylinder radius 2 cm and height 5 cm, volume is pi*2^2*5. At density 3 grams/cm^3, enter 3*pi*2^2*5 for mass.
rat-density.check: Density units must match the volume units. Distinguish radius from diameter and mass density from population per area.

rat-other.entry: If q units cost c dollars at a constant unit price, k units cost k*c/q. Test k=q to recover c and k=0 to recover zero.
rat-other.check: Requires q!=0 and direct proportionality. A fixed fee breaks this model; boundary tests do not alone prove the formula.

pct-of.entry: For 24 is p percent of 80, enter 100*24/80=30. For a count, 30% of 80 is entered as (30/100)*80.
pct-of.check: Identify the reference whole before dividing. A proportion 0.30 and a percent 30 have different requested forms.

pct-change.entry: If a value rises 20% then falls 10%, its multiplier is 1.2*0.9=1.08. Final 270 means original 270/(1.2*0.9)=250.
pct-change.check: Report net increase as 100(1.08-1)=8 percent. Reversal requires nonzero multipliers; a 100% decrease cannot be uniquely reversed.

1vd-mean.entry: Enter v=[0,1,2,3,4] and f=[2,5,4,3,1], then total(f*v)/total(f). For an ordinary raw list L, use mean(L).
1vd-mean.check: List multiplication is element by element. Frequencies must pair with their values and be nonnegative; total frequency must be positive.

1vd-median.entry: For values 0,1,2,3 with frequencies 2,3,4,1, cumulative counts are 2,5,9,10. Positions 5 and 6 hold 1 and 2, so median is 1.5.
1vd-median.check: Do not use median of the frequency list or unweighted category list. For even n average positions n/2 and n/2+1.

1vd-spread.entry: For raw data enter L=[1,2,2,5], then max(L)-min(L). Use stdevp(L) for population standard deviation or stdev(L) for sample standard deviation, as specified.
1vd-spread.check: Desmos stdev uses n-1; stdevp uses n. Comparing the two formulas across unequal sample sizes can change results. Translation preserves spread; multiplication by k scales standard deviation by abs(k).

1vd-change.choose: Hand: track mean and central positions separately
1vd-change.entry: For n values with mean m, adding z gives (n*m+z)/(n+1); removing z gives (n*m-z)/(n-1). For a median, re-index the sorted data after the edit.
1vd-change.check: Removing an extreme can change the median substantially when middle gaps are large: removing 1000 from [0,100,1000] changes the median from 100 to 50. The mean change also depends on n.

1vd-read.choose: Hand: recover only what the chart encodes
1vd-read.entry: For a dot plot, transcribe repeated values into a raw list and use mean(L) or median(L). For a box plot, read the median and quartiles directly; IQR=Q3-Q1.
